raw_case_text:
A 51-year-old man presented to the emergency department of the University Hospital of Basel, Switzerland with malaise, abdominal discomfort, floating yellow stool, jaundice and choluria of 4 days duration and a 6-8 kg weight loss over the last 6 weeks. He had returned from a 4 week trip to Ethiopia 3 weeks before seeking medical care. During his stay in Ethiopia, he consumed 1.25 g of Artemisia annua powder-tea on a daily basis as chemoprophylaxis for malaria. In about 90% of the cases he diluted the powder in boiling water, in the remaining 10% the powder was ingested mixed with food. The supplement had been purchased via the Internet. The patient provided us with the container, which had originally contained 50 g of a dark green powder (Figure 1). At presentation 2 g were in the container, indicating that he had consumed a total of 48 g. During his stay in Ethiopia, he had also consumed other tea-like preparations [black tea (Camellia sinensis) daily for breakfast, coffee-leaf tea (once) and rita graveolens tea (twice)]. To our knowledge, there is no described hepatotoxicity related to these substances. He denied taking any other prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal medications. He had no previous- or family history of liver disease, alcohol or drug abuse, or risk factors for viral hepatitis. He reported that his wife, who accompanied him on his trip to Ethiopia, had also consumed Artemesia annua tea for malaria prophylaxis. She remained well throughout.
Apart from marked jaundice, he was in a good general condition and had unremarkable vital signs (afebrile with normal blood pressure, heart rate and respiratory rate).
Laboratory tests showed: alanine aminotransferase (ALAT) 91 U/L (normal, 9-59); aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT) 42 U/L (normal, 9-34); alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 151 U/L (normal, 40-130); gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) 416 U/L (normal, 12-68); total bilirubin 186.6 mumol/L (normal, 0-24) (conjugated bilirubin 168.5 mumol/L); and international normalized ratio (INR) 0.9 (normal, 0.9-1.3). Bile acid level was elevated to al level of 460.5 mumol/L (normal, 0-8.0). Differential blood count and c-reactive protein were normal. Mild hyponatremia and hypochloremia were present, consistent with the patient's increased water intake over the previous days. Serological tests for acute hepatitis A, B, C and E, Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus infection were negative. Coeruloplasmin was normal. Liver-specific auto-antibodies (anti-nuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-proteinase 3 antibody and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody) were negative and IgA, IgM and IgG were within normal range. Abdominal ultrasonography showed a normal liver parenchyma, vessels and biliary ducts. The liver elastography was elevated (FibroScan, 12.7 kPa, normal range <5 kPa).
The patient was also evaluated at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute for various potential underlying infectious conditions. Antibodies against rickettsia spotted fever were positive, however, this was considered unrelated to the clinical presentation and no antibiotic therapy was started.
The initial liver biopsy showed a portal hepatitis with lymphocytic infiltration of the bile ducts and diffuse intra-canalicular and intra-cytoplasmic bilirubinostasis. Neither fibrosis nor parasitic material was seen (Figures 2A,B). A next generation sequencing analysis on DNA from peripheral blood leukocytes for genetic variants in the genes encoding the 3 most important hepatic transporters for bile acid homeostasis, namely BSEP, MDR3 and FIC1, found no variants typically associated with hereditary cholestatic liver diseases.
The toxicologic analysis of the Artemisia tea by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry and gas chromatography - mass spectrometry revealed the following ingredients: arteannuin b, deoxyartemisin, camphor and scopoletin.
Treatment with prednisone 20mg twice daily and ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily was initiated. Due to persistent jaundice as well as increasing bilirubin over 4 weeks despite treatment, a second liver biopsy was performed. The second biopsy showed a severe intracytoplasmatic as well as intracanalicular bilirubinostasis, with only minimal inflammation compared to the first biopsy (Figures 2C,D). Corticosteroid treatment was discontinued, ursodeoxycholic acid was continued until resolution of jaundice and normalization of bilirubin (15.3 mumol/l) (Figure 3) and relevant decrease of bile acids (19.5 mumol/l) which occurred three months after the disease's onset.
The case was reported to the pharmacovigilance unit of the Swiss national authority for therapeutic products (Swissmedic). Written informed consent was obtained from the participant for the publication of this case report.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of malaise, abdominal discomfort, floating yellow stools, jaundice, and dark urine (choluria), and a 6- to 8-kg weight loss over the preceding 6 weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three weeks after returning to Switzerland from a 4-week trip to Ethiopia—during which he consumed 1.25 g daily (48 g total) of an internet-purchased Artemisia annua powder tea for malaria chemoprophylaxis—the patient developed 4 days of malaise, abdominal discomfort, steatorrhea-like floating yellow stools, choluria, and frank jaundice alongside a 6-8 kg weight loss over 6 weeks.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical and family history; no prior liver disease. Social/travel history: 4-week trip to Ethiopia ending 3 weeks prior, where he ingested 48 g total of Artemisia annua herbal powder tea (plus black tea, coffee-leaf tea once, and Ruta graveolens tea twice); no alcohol or drug abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 4 days of malaise, abdominal discomfort, floating yellow stools, choluria, and jaundice, and 6 weeks of 6-8 kg weight loss. Denied prescription or OTC medications.

objective.physical_examination: Marked cutaneous and scleral jaundice in a patient in good general condition; afebrile with normal blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate.
objective.routine_investigations: ALT (ALAT) 91 U/L (normal 9-59), AST (ASAT) 42 U/L (normal 9-34), ALP 151 U/L (normal 40-130), GGT 416 U/L (normal 12-68), total bilirubin 186.6 umol/L (normal 0-24; conjugated bilirubin 168.5 umol/L; normalizing to 15.3 umol/L at 3 months), serum bile acids 460.5 umol/L (normal 0-8.0; decreasing to 19.5 umol/L at 3 months), INR 0.9 (normal 0.9-1.3), normal CBC and CRP, mild dilutional hyponatremia and hypochloremia, normal ceruloplasmin, and normal IgA, IgM, and IgG. Serologies for acute HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and cytomegalovirus (CMV) were all negative; Rickettsia spotted fever antibodies were positive (deemed incidental); liver autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA/anti-PR3/anti-MPO, ASMA, AMA) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver parenchyma, vessels, and bile ducts; FibroScan liver elastography was elevated at 12.7 kPa (normal <5 kPa).
objective.advanced_workup: Initial percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated portal hepatitis with lymphocytic bile duct infiltration and diffuse intracanalicular and intracytoplasmic bilirubinostasis without fibrosis or parasites; repeat liver biopsy at 4 weeks showed severe intracytoplasmic and intracanalicular bilirubinostasis with minimal residual inflammation. Next-generation sequencing of BSEP, MDR3, and FIC1 excluded hereditary cholestatic liver diseases. LC-MS and GC-MS toxicological analysis of the Artemisia annua powder identified arteannuin B, deoxyartemisinin, camphor, and scopoletin.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with severe prolonged cholestatic drug/herbal-induced liver injury (DILI) secondary to Artemisia annua herbal tea ingestion, confirmed by two liver biopsies demonstrating severe intracanalicular and intracytoplasmic bilirubinostasis, LC-MS/GC-MS chemical analysis of the ingested powder, and exclusion of viral hepatitis A/B/C/E, CMV, EBV, autoimmune liver disease, biliary obstruction, and hereditary BSEP/MDR3/FIC1 transporter defects. Treated initially with oral prednisone (20 mg BID, discontinued after week 4 repeat biopsy) and oral ursodeoxycholic acid (500 mg BID), achieving complete resolution of jaundice and normalization of bilirubin (15.3 umol/L) and bile acids (19.5 umol/L) at 3 months.
